meta.title: Who really said "Applause is the spur of noble minds, the end and aim of weak ones"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Edmund Burke. The line is an aphorism in Charles Caleb Colton’s Lacon, Vol. I (1820) — confirmed in the scanned 1824 and 1836 printings.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Applause is the spur of noble minds, the end and aim of weak ones'?
meta.ogDescription: Credited to Edmund Burke all over the internet. It is Charles Caleb Colton, Lacon Vol. I (1820) — verified in two nineteenth-century scans.

answer.label: Not Edmund Burke — actually Charles Caleb Colton
answer.sourceLine: The sentence is a numbered aphorism in Colton’s Lacon; or, Many Things in Few Words, Volume I of which was first published in 1820. The wording that circulates today is exact — it appears verbatim in the scanned New York printing of 1824 (“from the eighth London edition”) and again in the 1836 New York edition. Edmund Burke died in 1797, before Lacon existed.

source.excerpt: Applause is the spur of noble minds, the end and aim of weak ones.
trail: Start with the specialists. Wikiquote’s Applause page ↗ carries the sentence and credits it to Charles Caleb Colton, Lacon (1820) — not to Burke. Quote Investigator has no article on this line.
Locate it in the book. Wikiquote’s Colton page ↗ files it under Volume I, § CCCCXXIV, and the independent WIST quotation database ↗ gives the same placement, Lacon Vol. 1, § 424 (1820).
Read the primary text. The full scan of the New York 1824 printing, taken from the eighth London edition ↗, carries the sentence verbatim as aphorism CCCCXXIII on p. 181.

Check a second printing. The 1836 New York edition ↗ has the identical wording in the identical position, between the passages on public charities and on quarrels — so this is Colton’s text, not a printer’s stray.
source.excerptNote: Lacon is a book of free-standing numbered aphorisms, so there is no larger passage to quote — the sentence is the whole entry. In the 1824 printing it sits between Colton’s reflection on public charities and his remark that “in most quarrels there is a fault on both sides.”

author.name: Charles Caleb Colton
author.heading: Who was Charles Caleb Colton?
author.bio: Charles Caleb Colton was an English clergyman and writer whose one enduring book, Lacon; or, Many Things in Few Words, is a collection of numbered aphorisms — Volume I appeared in 1820, Volume II in 1822. He was known as much for his eccentricity as his prose: a wine dealer, gambler and collector who eventually left England for Paris. His own works are now almost forgotten, and he survives mainly through quotation anthologies — which is precisely how his lines end up drifting onto other people’s names.

misattribution.heading: How Burke got the credit
misattribution.intro: Search the line today and Edmund Burke’s name comes back first. No edition of Burke contains it, and no quotation site crediting him offers a work, speech or page — the attribution travels on repetition alone.

items.why: Large aggregator sites file the sentence under Burke with no source attached — A-Z Quotes lists it on its Applause page as Burke ↗, and QuoteFancy carries it in its Edmund Burke collection ↗. The chronology alone rules it out: Burke died in 1797 ↗, and the first volume of Lacon was published in 1820 ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The sentence is Colton’s. It stands as a numbered aphorism in the 1824 printing of Lacon ↗, between his passage on public charities and his passage on quarrels — exactly where Wikiquote places it in Volume I ↗.

context.heading: Why this one drifted
lead: Lacon was built to be quoted. Colton wrote in short, numbered, self-contained hits — hundreds of them — with no argument running between them, which made the book perfect raw material for the Victorian anthologies that came after. That is a blessing for circulation and a curse for provenance: once a sentence is lifted out of a numbered list, nothing about it says who wrote it.

Edmund Burke is the kind of name such orphaned lines land on. He is famous, quotable, and already carries more attributed aphorisms than he ever wrote — so a crisp epigram about applause and weak minds slots in without anyone blinking. The tell is the calendar: Burke died in 1797, and Lacon’s first volume did not appear until 1820.
context.detailsSummary: A note on the aphorism number
detailsBody: Colton’s aphorisms are numbered in Roman numerals, and the numbering is not identical across editions and reprints. In the 1824 New York printing consulted here the sentence stands as CCCCXXIII on p. 181; Wikiquote’s Colton page and the WIST quotation database both file it as Volume I, § CCCCXXIV (424). The text either side of it — the passage on public charities before, the passage on quarrels after — is the same in every printing checked, so the sentence’s position in the book is not in doubt.
context.pull: Colton wrote to be excerpted — which is exactly how his name got left behind.
